initial.prompt: Use case: style-transfer. Edit the supplied photograph into a clear technical pen-and-ink illustration for a French vintage typewriter installation manual, like a patent drawing or an original 1980s instruction manual. The photo is the mechanical source of truth. Preserve its viewing direction, proportions, and the positions of the real parts; do not mirror or redesign anything. Black contours on a plain white opaque background, restrained fine hatching only for depth, no photorealistic texture, no tablecloth, no shadows or dirt. The keyboard, case, sockets and relevant parts must remain recognizable. Only annotation arrows may use color. Avoid tiny unreadable labels: simplify unimportant legends instead of inventing text. Preserve complete requested assembly within the frame, with margins. No invented hands, tools, screws or clips. This is the complete typewriter with its paper support raised and printing mechanism exposed. Precisely preserve the FOUR red arrows and their screw-hole targets: rear-left, rear-right, left beside the LCD and right beside the LCD. Label these arrows A, B, C, D respectively, in small clear black letters. Precisely preserve the FIVE yellow arrows and their plastic clip targets and inward pressure directions: left side inward, right side inward, front-left inward, front-middle inward, front-right inward. Label them 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 respectively. Re-render arrows as clean simple technical arrows; do not add more arrows, screws, or clips. Keep red and yellow saturated and easy to distinguish. White keyboard key tops and black outlines, not a dark textured photographic keyboard. No headline or paragraph text. Exactly 4 red arrows and 5 yellow arrows.

corrections.prompt: Edit this existing technical drawing only in two arrow tips. Preserve the complete black-and-white drawing, all other arrows, the 4 red arrows, 5 yellow arrows, letters and numbers exactly. The red arrows C and D currently stop on the narrow rectangular notches beside the screws. Extend C slightly right so its tip points directly at the CENTER of the round screw hole just right of its current tip. Extend D slightly left so its tip points directly at the CENTER of the round screw hole just left of its current tip. Keep these two red arrows horizontal and their letters C and D outside the machine. Do not redraw, reposition or add any other mechanical detail. Keep plain opaque white background.

Edit this existing patent-style drawing only by removing the 5 circular number labels (1, 2, 3, 4, 5) at the tails of the yellow arrows. Keep the FIVE yellow arrows themselves, their original directions and exact tips on the clips. Keep every black-and-white plastic case detail unchanged. The removed labels must be replaced with plain white background. Do not add words, number labels, extra arrows or anything else. Preserve the frame and orientation.

final_demontage_prompt: Edit this technical drawing, keeping all black-and-white mechanical geometry and the five numbered yellow arrows unchanged. Replace ALL FOUR red screw arrows with FOUR RED CIRCULAR RINGS that surround the actual round screw heads, labelled A, B, C and D nearby in black. Ring A: the round recessed screw on the upper rear horizontal rail, below old arrow A. Ring B: the round recessed screw on the upper rear rail, below old arrow B. Ring C: the ROUND recessed screw immediately left of the two left control-button pairs and left of the LCD, to the RIGHT of the old arrow C tip. Ring D: the ROUND recessed screw immediately right of the two right control-button pairs, to the LEFT of the old arrow D tip. For C and D do NOT mark the rectangular slots in the outer frame, which are clips, not screws. Delete the old red arrows completely. Each red ring should surround the outer circular screw recess without covering its hole, leaving the screw readable. Exactly four red rings, two at the rear and two beside the LCD, and five yellow clip arrows. No new mechanical features. Plain opaque white background. These red rings will give novice readers an unambiguous screw location.
